[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the Current Population Survey (CPS) or similar matched employer-employee datasets, analyzing firm-level training expenditures by profit margin quartiles before and after state-level minimum wage increases above inflation. — This would directly test the differential effect of minimum wage hikes on training investment across firms with varying profit margins, controlling for time trends and firm characteristics.

[PATH:empirical] Field experiment or quasi-experimental study in high-productivity urban markets (e.g., major U.S. cities) comparing training hours and costs between low-margin and high-margin firms following a legislated minimum wage increase. — A natural or controlled experiment would provide causal evidence on whether low-margin firms reduce training while high-margin firms increase it, addressing the core conditional claim.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing labor economics literature on minimum wage effects, focusing on studies that report firm-level training outcomes and profit margins as moderators. — Synthesizing prior empirical findings can reveal whether the hypothesized pattern is consistently observed across different contexts, helping confirm or refute the conditional hypothesis.
